summary: A BBN note that the link field in the IMP/Host leader was widened by four bits and renamed the message-id field, so hosts could identify individual messages more uniquely and get more throughput. All 12 bits are returned in RFNMs and similar replies. Hosts need not use the extra bits.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 533 expands a field in IMP/Host messages so hosts can identify individual messages more clearly. Hosts can ignore the added bits, and the field does not say what order messages have.

questions: what is the imp message-id field
how many bits is the message-id in the imp host leader
is the message-id change backward compatible
subtitle: A wider IMP/Host field that can identify individual messages rather than only links.

tldr.problem: Identifying messages only by the link number constrained throughput when hosts needed to distinguish messages.
tldr.mechanism: The IMP/Host and Host/IMP leader link field is extended by four bits and renamed message-id; all 12 bits are returned to the host in responses such as RFNMs.
tldr.outcome: Hosts may use the extra bits to identify messages, but are not required to do so. The RFC says the change is backward compatible and does not imply message ordering.

today: The unit records RFC 533's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. The RFC asks readers to keep it with BBN Report 1822 until that report is updated.

sections.title: Why Change the Link Field
sections.content:
The IMP message format in BBN Report 1822 uses a link field. RFC 533 says that uniquely identifying messages through the link number limits throughput.

BBN reports that it has changed the IMP/Host protocol to address this limit. The change expands the field used in both IMP/Host and Host/IMP leaders.
sections.plainLanguage: A link number did not give hosts enough room to identify messages while sending at higher throughput. The RFC describes a wider field for message identifiers.

sections.title: The Message-ID Field
sections.content:
The link field is extended to the right by four bits and renamed the message-id field. It occupies bits 17 through 28 of the leader, for a total of 12 bits. The RFC expects hosts to use it to identify messages between IMPs and hosts.

All 12 bits are returned to the host in RFNMs, incomplete transmissions and similar responses. The RFC explicitly says that message-id values do not imply an ordering.
sections.plainLanguage: The field is now 12 bits wide and comes back in responses. It can identify a message, but it does not tell the host which message came first.

sections.title: Optional Use and Compatibility
sections.content:
Because the Host/Host protocol already uses the old link field to identify connections, hosts could use the additional four bits to identify messages within one connection. The RFC says hosts are not obligated to uniquely identify their messages, and the IMP subnetwork does not depend on that use.

A receiving host need not examine the extra bits. The RFC therefore describes the change as backward compatible even when a sending host uses those bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts may use the extra bits or ignore them. Older receivers can still work because they do not have to inspect the new portion of the field.
